articles.title_orig: Diriba breaks course record, Berhanu threatens mark at Amsterdam Marathon
articles.title_zh: Diriba breaks course record, Berhanu threatens mark at Amsterdam Marathon
articles.content_orig:
Lemi Berhanu wins the TCS Amsterdam Marathon ( © Getty Images )
Buze Diriba ran a course record of 2:16:12 and Lemi Berhanu threatened the men’s mark by running 2:03:33 to win at the TCS Amsterdam Marathon, a World Athletics Platinum Label road race, on Sunday (18).
Racing in wet conditions, both clocked impressive negative splits to achieve big PBs. Ethiopia’s Diriba improved on her previous best of 2:19:34 to break the course record and Dutch all-comers' record of 2:16:52 set by Yalemzerf Yehualaw in 2024, while her compatriot Berhanu, the 2016 Boston Marathon champion, continued his resurgence by taking a minute off his PB set in January, missing the course record by just three seconds.
Diriba was followed by defending champion Aynalem Desta, who ran a PB of 2:17:06, while Meseret Belete completed an Ethiopian top three in 2:18:06, also a PB.
Kenya’s Nicholas Kipkorir, who claimed world half marathon silver in Copenhagen last month, chased Berhanu over the finish line to secure another runner-up finish in a big PB of 2:03:39, while his Kenyan compatriot Patrick Mosin was third in a PB of 2:03:58 as the top eight all dipped under 2:05.
Diriba and Desta were always to the fore in the women’s race and they were joined by Mestawut Fikir and Belete as the halfway point was reached in 1:08:34.
They hit the 30-kilometre mark in 1:37:23 before Fikir was dropped, losing 17 seconds on the leaders over the next kilometre.
Desta and Diriba forged on, creating a gap on Belete, and then Diriba kicked. She was half a minute ahead by 40km and increased that advantage to almost a minute by the finish.
Diriba has now broken 2:20 in three marathons during the past 12 months – she ran her previous best of 2:19:34 to win in Frankfurt last October before clocking 2:19:54 to place second in Daegu in February. By running 2:16:12 in Amsterdam, the 32-year-old moved to 16th on the world all-time list.
Buze Diriba celebrates her TCS Amsterdam Marathon win (© Getty Images)
Behind the top three, Tiringo Mulu finished fourth in 2:20:36 and Fikir was fifth in 2:21:32.
The men’s race also set off outside course record pace, but a strong finish took Berhanu to within three seconds of the mark set by Geofry Toroitich Kipchumba last year.
A large lead group remained together at halfway, headed by the pacemakers in 1:02:24. Kipchumba, defending his title, was eight seconds back at that point and he dropped out a short while later.
Kenya’s Justus Kangogo took control as the pacemakers stepped aside at the 30-kilometre mark, reached in 1:28:48. The pack stretched out as he picked up the pace, reaching the 35-kilometre checkpoint in 1:43:23, joined at the front by Mosin, Kipkorir, and Jonathan Korir, with Berhanu a stride back.
A big move was made as they approached the Vondelpark, as Kipkorir kicked and Berhanu went with him, leaving their rivals behind. They were shoulder to shoulder as they hit the 40-kilometre mark in 1:57:25, 11 seconds ahead of Mosin.
Then Berhanu edged ahead and Kipkorir could not respond, looking over his shoulder as he ran in second place.
Berhanu was well clear as he returned to the Olympic Stadium for the final stretch, striding over the finish line in 2:03:33 to secure a six-second victory. In only his second marathon, Kipkorir improved on the 2:06:07 he ran on his debut in Boston in April to secure the runner-up spot, while Mosin was third, another 19 seconds back.
Kalipus Lomwai was fourth (2:04:08), Sila Kiptoo fifth (2:04:12) and Kangogo sixth (2:04:24). Korir and Isaia Kipkoech Lasoi, the latter making his marathon debut, also finished inside 2:05. It is only the third race in history in which eight men have broken the 2:05 mark.

articles.title_orig: TSLA, CSIQ Stocks In Focus As China Tightens Solar Manufacturing Technology Exports
articles.title_zh: TSLA, CSIQ Stocks In Focus As China Tightens Solar Manufacturing Technology Exports
articles.content_orig:
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Shares of Tesla Inc. (TSLA) and Canadian Solar Inc. (CSIQ) are in focus after China proposed tighter controls on the export of technologies used to manufacture solar panels and cells.
China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology on Friday proposed adding 12 photovoltaic technologies to the country's export-control list, including technologies related to polysilicon, silicon wafers and advanced solar-cell manufacturing, per a report by Reuters.
Tesla shares closed 2% lower on Friday, while Canadian Solar shares fell more than 7%.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Under the proposal, China would prohibit exports of certain technologies used to manufacture perovskite and tandem solar cells, as well as selected thin-silicon wafer and fluidized-bed polysilicon technologies. Other advanced manufacturing technologies, including TOPCon, HJT and back-contact technologies, would face restrictions rather than an outright export ban.
The measures are part of a broader revision of China's Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export. Beijing said the photovoltaic additions cover technologies used in polysilicon manufacturing, silicon-wafer manufacturing and solar-cell manufacturing.
China's Commerce Ministry said the move is aimed at addressing national security concerns, pointing to the growing use of photovoltaic technologies in areas including aerospace, national defense, unmanned equipment and high-security infrastructure.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
“The national security risks that may be caused by the export of solar technology have been constantly rising. It is necessary to implement timely and appropriate supervision,” the ministry said.
At the same time, Beijing stressed that the controls are intended to be narrowly targeted. The ministry said technologies that do not meet the specified control thresholds would remain freely exportable and that products manufactured using controlled technologies are not themselves within the scope of the proposed rules.
"The scope of technologies listed in this announcement is limited; other technologies that do not meet the control indicators can still be freely exported," the ministry said.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
According to a Reuters report from March, Tesla was in talks with Chinese firms to procure about $2.9 billion worth of solar manufacturing equipment, including equipment from Suzhou Maxwell Technologies, Shenzhen S.C New Energy Technology and Laplace Renewable Energy Technology.
Tesla CEO Elon Musk outlined his vision at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January this year, with the EV giant planning to add 100 GW of solar manufacturing capacity in the U.S. by 2028.
Canadian Solar could be particularly relevant because its U.S. manufacturing expansion relies on heterojunction technology, or HJT, one of the advanced solar-cell technologies specifically identified for export restrictions under China's proposal.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Canadian Solar's subsidiary CS PowerTech officially opened the first phase of its HJT solar-cell factory in Jeffersonville, Indiana, earlier this year. The first phase has a total capacity of 2.1 GW, while a second phase is expected to bring total U.S. cell capacity to 6.3 GW in the first half of 2027.
The company has described the Indiana facility as the first U.S. plant designed to produce advanced HJT bifacial N-type solar cells. Together with its Texas module facility, the expansion is intended to create a more localized U.S. solar manufacturing supply chain.
"We are executing on a multidimensional solar technology roadmap, spanning advanced cell innovations to next-generation applications," Canadian Solar CEO Colin Parkin said in August. "In the near to midterm, U.S. manufacturing remains at the forefront of our strategy."
Advertisement | Remove ads.
However, the proposal does not mean that Canadian Solar's HJT factory is automatically blocked. China's Commerce Ministry emphasized that the controls have specific technical indicators and that only technologies and key equipment meeting those thresholds would be subject to the proposed restrictions.
Retail sentiment on Stocktwits around Tesla trended in the ‘bullish’ territory at the time of writing.
TSLA stock is down 21% year-to-date, while CSIQ stock is down 59%. The S&P 500 ETF (SPY) is up 16% over the past 12 months, while the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) is up 18%.

articles.title_orig: India’s Middle Power Problem: Hedging Between Russia’s Decline and China’s Rise
articles.title_zh: India’s Middle Power Problem: Hedging Between Russia’s Decline and China’s Rise
articles.content_orig:
In an effort to be in compliance with GDPR we are providing you with the latest documentation about how we collect, use, share and secure your information, we want to make you aware of our updated privacy policy here
In 2026 India concluded a free trade agreement with the European Union, struck an interim tariff deal with the United States, absorbed a Gulf war that upended its oil supply, sent its air force to train with Japanese fighters, and hosted both Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping at a BRICS summit in New Delhi. Eleven days before welcoming Putin, Narendra Modi had told him in Bishkek that the world must move from endless war to an end to the war.
Taken one at a time these are episodes. Taken together they describe a state working every relationship at once. My two recent articles argued that this is hedging rather than realignment. India is thinning its dependence on Russia at the margin while keeping the installed Russian base, buying Russian oil when supply and price justify it, and building partners elsewhere.
This article asks what that pattern means for India as a middle power. It uses the framework Kenneth Maxwell and I developed in The Australian, Brazilian and Chinese Dynamic . My argument is that the Russia hedge is a subordinate move in a larger game. The principal problem is China. Russia matters to India less as a partner than as a counterweight, and as a warning about what China’s informal empire does to a partner it has weakened.
Three findings carry over. First, India’s Russia relationship must be read as stock and flow. The share of new arms deliveries from Russia has fallen from 70 to 40 per cent over a decade, while the installed base remains overwhelmingly Russian in origin. Second, India layers rather than exits. It refused the Su-57 and is upgrading the Su-30MKI with Indian sensors and weapons, but it also ordered more S-400s. Third, Russian oil is a portfolio position, driven by Gulf disruption, Russian supply and American pressure rather than by sentiment about Ukraine.
The Ukraine book supplies the frame around these findings. Putin’s war has shrunk Russia’s reach and made it a junior partner of China. India is the largest Global South customer whose choices decide how far that subordination goes. Its interest is not simply to reduce Russian exposure but to keep Russia from becoming wholly dependent on Beijing while it reduces its own.
Our book offers four ideas that matter here.
Informal empire. Following Gallagher and Robinson’s 1953 concept, we argued that China builds influence through trade, investment, ports, finance and a Global South narrative rather than formal control. Latin America was our main case, but the method is general. It creates dependence through commerce and then converts dependence into political leverage.
Two models. Australia leans toward security when forced to choose. It accepts economic costs, banned Huawei from its 5G network, and built a deterrence-focused defense posture around the alliance with the United States. Brazil practices strategic pragmatism. It embraces Chinese trade, uses BRICS to expand its autonomy, and signed a cooperation plan linking its programs to the Belt and Road rather than joining the initiative formally. We explained the divergence through geography, alliance commitments, history and economic structure.
Hedging as the norm. Both countries hedge, in different versions, and we argued this is becoming normal for middle powers rather than exceptional. We also noted that Beijing courts middle powers with a multi-alignment strategy of its own, encouraging cooperative relations with several powers rather than exclusive alignment. Hedging does not threaten China’s informal empire unless it is backed by capability.
Capability, resolve and signalling. Air Marshal Chipman’s framing of deterrence as capability multiplied by resolve multiplied by signalling, where a zero in any term makes the product zero, applies to any middle power facing a larger neighbor. Resolve, he argued, is a whole-of-society problem that includes economic relationships with the adversary.
By the book’s material definition, India does not qualify. It describes middle powers as economies ranking roughly twentieth to thirtieth, while India’s economy is far larger, and India is nuclear-armed with 1.4 billion people. Yet the book’s concluding chapter lists “the Indians” among the significant middle powers, and the functional definition makes sense. A middle power is a state that cannot decide the order alone and must shape it through partnerships, institutions and selective capabilities. India fits that description relative to the United States and China.
India is a third case that combines features of both of our models. Like Australia, it faces a direct security problem with China. It has a contested land border, the 2020 Galwan clash, and a Chinese military build-up on the Line of Actual Control. Like Brazil, it insists on strategic autonomy, chairs BRICS, and refuses to become a treaty ally. Unlike both, it has neither an alliance guarantee nor Brazil’s geographic distance. Its Russian ties give it a hedge that neither Australia nor Brazil possesses.
The clearest sign is trade. The latest reporting puts India’s trade deficit with China above $112 billion, the widest on record, with imports over $130 billion against exports under $20 billion. Another account says India buys about seven dollars of Chinese goods for every dollar it sells, in a relationship where trade has nearly doubled in five years. Much of this is organic, driven by Chinese price and technology competitiveness, which is exactly how informal empire works. Dependence grows through commerce that appears voluntary.
Leverage follows dependence. Over 90 per cent of India’s rare earth magnets and metals came from China, and Chinese rare earth magnet exports to India fell 58 per cent after January 2025. Earlier this year China also restricted imports of Indian rice and chilli. India’s response includes a Rs 7,280 crore magnet manufacturing scheme approved in November 2025 and rare earth corridors announced in the 2026-27 Budget. These are the right measures, but their effects will take years.
Australia’s experience is instructive. Babbage’s argument in our book is that Chinese coercion of Australia was a “sovereignty war” rather than a trade dispute, and that resilience means diversifying markets and supply chains. A study by Laurenceson that we quote finds that Australia’s interests were protected not by geopolitical friends but by interdependence that constrained Beijing and by access to a rules-based trading system. Diversification worked because alternatives existed.
Russia is the negative example. As the Ukraine book shows, China has made Russia a price-taker, moved it into the yuan, and captured its Far East and Central Asian markets. India has a direct interest in avoiding a similar path.
India has spent 2026 building alternatives, and the record shows a familiar hedging style.
On February 2 President Trump announced a deal cutting US tariffs on Indian goods to 18 per cent and said Modi had agreed to stop buying Russian oil. The joint statement did not mention Russian oil, and the Indian government has neither confirmed nor denied the pledge, saying its purchases are guided by national interest. An executive order provides that a 25 per cent tariff would return if India resumes such purchases. Indian refiners meanwhile avoided Russian cargoes for March and April, and Russian crude’s share of Indian imports had already fallen from a 40 per cent peak to under 25 per cent by December.
Then the Iran war began on February 28. India’s Russian oil share went from 18.7 per cent in February to nearly 50 per cent in July, as its Middle East imports fell by 63 per cent. I have not found reporting that the US has reimposed the tariff, although Senate pressure for tariffs on buyers of Russian energy is growing. The sequence looks like textbook hedging

articles.title_orig: Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition
articles.title_zh: Why stealing pumpkins for newlyweds is a blessing in ancient Chinese tradition
articles.content_orig:
Some northern communities traditionally place a pumpkin under the wedding quilt as a blessing for future generations
In ancient China, welcoming autumn could involve stealing pumpkins, sitting on giant hanging scales and eating extra meat – rituals reflecting how people connected seasonal change with fertility, health and good fortune.
Historical records show that during the Qing dynasty (1644–1912), groups of young people would gather on the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival to sneak into fields and take pumpkins.
Far from being considered wrongdoing, the practice was often tolerated – and even welcomed – by farmers. By the Republican era (1912–1949), it had become particularly prevalent in rural communities.

articles.title_zh: Qian Jiang, former Johns Hopkins’ eye institute expert, joins Chinese hospital
articles.content_orig:
Chinese specialist leaves US for Sir Run Run Shaw Hospital to research eye transplants and work on virtual cells to test drug responses
Professor Qian Jiang, a senior eye expert at Johns Hopkins University in the United States, has moved back to China full time to pursue research on eye transplants.
At the ceremony, Qian said he would also work on “virtual cells” – computer models that mimic real cells so scientists can test how they might respond to drugs or disease without lab experiments.

articles.title_orig: China to limit exports of 40 key technologies, including AI and solar
articles.title_zh: China to limit exports of 40 key technologies, including AI and solar
articles.content_orig:
China's Ministry of Commerce has released a draft plan for export limits on 40 key technologies in artificial intelligence (AI), photovoltaics and biomedicine.
The export of 14 of these technologies is to be banned, while the other 26 will require approval. The new bans and approval requirements have not yet been finalized. Comments can be submitted until November 15.
However, since the announcement was published on Friday, companies have been required to register affected technology transfers. Such transfers include selling intellectual property rights and granting licences abroad.
The focus is on 23 AI technologies. These include methods for large AI models and AI agents, which perform tasks largely autonomously. Further plans concern manufacturing processes for solar cells and techniques for cell and gene therapies.
Access to AI services via apps and websites is to remain exempt from the new export limits, according to the ministry. This also applies to AI technologies that are already publicly available.
In solar technology, individual production facilities are covered, but finished solar modules will not fall under the planned controls.
The Ministry of Commerce cited security risks. AI could be used for attacks on important infrastructure. Solar technology is also used in space and defence. The measures are not aimed at specific countries or companies.
China had already restricted certain processes for making battery materials and extracting lithium in 2025. Approval requirements were also introduced for certain rare earths and products made from them.
The new move falls into the technology rivalry with the United States, which in turn controls exports of advanced AI chips to China.

articles.title_orig: 4 Takeaways From a Voting-Focused ‘No Kings’ Day
articles.title_zh: 4 Takeaways From a Voting-Focused ‘No Kings’ Day
articles.content_orig:
Hundreds of demonstrators rallied and marched near the Colorado Capitol on Saturday in the largest of dozens of planned No Kings events across the state, part of a nationwide day of action that organizers hope will encourage participants to vote and help protect the November election.
It was the latest in a series of No Kings events since President Donald Trump’s inauguration in January 2025. Protesters say the Trump administration has pursued authoritarian policies, such as disregard for the rule of law, abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and attempts to meddle in elections.
Nita Gonzales, daughter of Denver Chicano activist Corky Gonzales and a longtime activist herself, addressed a crowd of hundreds of demonstrators gathered on the Capitol grounds and across Civic Center Park.
“Does this look like hopelessness? This looks like courage,” Gonzales said from the Capitol steps. “This looks like democracy. This looks like people reclaiming their voice and their power.”
Christy Aguilar, an organizer of the Denver rally, told Newsline she wanted the event to engage and represent Colorado’s Latino community in a way that previous events hadn’t.
“I’ve noticed the lack of Latino power in No Kings planning, I’ve noticed (the) Latino population not coming out to No Kings,” Aguilar said. “So this was my way of trying to get my community to come out and get them more involved in the polls, get them more informed of what’s going on. Because everything that’s on the ballot is affecting us personally.”
Nationwide, Saturday’s No Kings protests were focused on mobilizing voters to make a plan for heading to the polls, and to vote early if possible. National No Kings organizers were joined at a press conference in Washington earlier this week by Bishop William Barber, founder of the social justice group Repairers of the Breach and co-chair of the Poor People’s Campaign, who has organized 652 early-voting marches in 428 locations across the country this year.
Under Colorado’s universal vote-by-mail system, ballots were mailed to all active registered voters in the state beginning Oct. 2. Voters may submit completed ballots by mail or at a drop box or voting center. They may also vote in-person at a voting center. Eligible voters can visit GoVoteColorado.gov for more information and to check their registration status.
In an interview, Gonzales said the consequences of Trump’s actions over the last decade have been been “horrific” for the Latino community and beyond.
“I’m a grandmother,” she said. “I don’t want my grandchild being raised in this kind of environment, where those that have more get more, and those that have less are at the bottom of of the rung and not able to have a life that they deserve to have. So then I get angry.”
Mark Lyons of Centennial told Newsline he hadn’t been involved in much political activism or organizing before last year. Saturday’s protest was his fourth No Kings event.
“I thought it’s time to get involved, it’s time to make a difference,” Lyons said. “It’s a community, and a lot of like-minded people, coming together for a common goal.”
I’m a grandmother ... I don’t want my grandchild being raised in this kind of environment, where those that have more get more, and those that have less are at the bottom of of the rung and not able to have a life that they deserve to have. So then I get angry.
– Nita Gonzales, at the No Kings protest
With the midterms approaching, Lyons is hopeful that Democrats will take back Congress and “put all kinds of checks and balances” on the Trump administration.
“They’ve been stealing the country blind for the last two years,” he said. “There has to be accountability, and it can’t be business as usual.”
No Kings event in Grand Junction emphasizes early voting, nonpartisan participation
Protests in Colorado were planned in numerous locations throughout the Denver area, and in cities such as Fort Collins, Boulder, Colorado Springs, Pueblo, Grand Junction and Durango.
“The No Kings movement stands ready to mobilize in response to attacks on our elections,” the No Kings website says. “By signing the No Kings pledge, you commit to be part of the solution, ready to join mass nonviolent action in rapid response to election disruption and subversion if needed.”
Aly Belknap, executive director of Colorado Common Cause, urged rally-goers to help “defend the vote” against the lies about widespread voter fraud promoted by Trump and many other Republicans. Her organization is leading a coalition of groups that are training nonpartisan, volunteer poll monitors to observe polling sites and drop boxes to protect against subversion next month.
“We know that we have debunked this lie over and over and over, and yet these are the lies that constitute what our neighbors and our family members and even our friends have been drawn in to believe,” Belknap said. “Why? … (Because) the people in power, they would like to decide who wins.”
Gonzales told the crowd to vote — “and then after you vote,” she added, “you get yourself out to defend your neighbors and communities, and stand up against ICE.”
“Voting is step one, but it is also about continuing to be active in neighborhoods and communities, to defend your neighbors, stand up, whatever that call comes, and not become complacent,” Gonzales told Newsline. “That’s what went wrong — we got complacent. We have to be vigilant, and we have to protect democracy and freedom, and that means standing up.”

articles.title_orig: What brought a Chinese desert fighter and an American teacher together?
articles.title_zh: What brought a Chinese desert fighter and an American teacher together?
articles.content_orig:
It was Oct 15, and I was at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome, witnessing FAO honor 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development. Ninety-nine names had been published on its website well in advance, but the organizers had kept the final recipient a secret.
It was a clever but also risky decision, I have to say. Keeping the name secret would help attract global attention, but whoever was chosen would have to live up to the expectations created by such an unusual announcement.
My doubts disappeared the moment the name and photograph of Yin Yuzhen appeared on the giant screen. Huge applause erupted. Journalists and delegates alike rushed forward, hoping to catch a closer glimpse of the Chinese woman who had devoted decades to fighting desertification. The applause quickly turned into a rhythm, with people chanting her name in different accents.
Accompanied by FAO director-general Qu Dongyu, Yin made her way onto the stage.
There she was, standing before an international audience, looking much as she might have looked back home in the countryside of northern China, wearing a dark green top and gray-black trousers. She struggled to work two English words, "brother" and "sister", into her Mandarin acceptance speech, but with such a heavy accent that few caught them.
But that didn't matter. Everyone in the hall knew her story with 8 million trees planted at the Mu Us Sandy Land, an achievement whose weight everyone understood beyond words.
Ronald Sakolsky, a retired American teacher who helped her in the 1990s and kept a 27-year-long friendship with her, joined her. Qu joked that Sakolsky was not eligible for an award honoring women, but had prepared a special souvenir for him.
Sakolsky laughed along with everyone else, but soon found himself in tears as he looked back on how they first met and what they had achieved together. The two spoke onstage, revisiting their past, reflecting on the present and imagining the future, thus turning the ceremony into a deeply moving reunion.
Yet for me, it also raised a question: Yin and Sakolsky's first encounter lasted only a few days, during which Sakolsky, having raised $5,000 for tree planting, visited her to see how she did it. Sakolsky eventually returned to his own life, while Yin went back to planting trees. They did not see each other again for 27 years, until they reunited in China earlier this year.
Yet when they met again, the warmth and understanding between them seemed entirely undiminished.
How could two people who had spent so little time together, and then stayed apart for nearly three decades, still share such a powerful connection?
After interviewing both of them, I think I found the answer: They are both idealists. OK, if the word appears too grand, let's call them people determined to do things well.
A rural woman confronting a desert, Yin has known since the first day she planted trees that every additional tree meant a little more greenery and a little less sand. She has never been taught any grand environmental theory; yet she never lost the belief that if she kept working, the landscape around her could eventually change.
Sakolsky, an American teacher, heard about someone trying to make the planet a better place. He believed such an effort deserved support, even if the person undertaking it lived thousands of kilometers from his home.
For Yin, planting trees was simply the right thing to do. For Sakolsky, helping someone plant them was equally obvious.
In a sense, both were stubborn. Once they had decided what was worth doing, they were determined to do it.
That's what linked them together, across national boundaries, languages and cultures. Such a friendship doesn't need frequent meetings, shared professional interests or expectations of personal reward. It is sustained by a shared belief that ordinary people can improve the world through their own actions.
More importantly, idealism, or the strong belief that one can do things well, is contagious. In our exclusive interview, when recalling 1999, Sakolsky said that he didn't think Yin could succeed until he saw what she was doing with his own eyes. And he is not the only one inspired by Yin, who said the award not only belongs to her alone, but also to the many "brothers and sisters" who helped.
Those "brothers and sisters" include people from the local government, nearby communities, and volunteers from over 20 countries and regions. Many didn't believe someone could plant trees in the sandy land first, but later joined Yin in her resolve.
They, too, were inspired by Yin, and have become idealists ready to inspire others.
Perhaps after spending so much of her life planting trees, Yin simply cannot stop. On Oct 16, the day after the ceremony, she joined Sakolsky and Qu in planting another tree at FAO headquarters.
It was World Food Day, and delegates attending the celebrations gathered around, eager to see this legendary Chinese desert fighter at work. Hopefully, when they return home, more people will continue the path of inspiration.
Of course, not everyone has the opportunity to meet Yin in person, but perhaps that is not necessary. Everyone who continues working toward a worthwhile ideal, however modest the effort may seem, carries something of the same spirit.
And every tree planted, wherever it grows, is another reminder that the world can be made a little better by people who believe it is worth trying.

articles.title_orig: From Pius XI to Leo XIV: World Mission Day marks 100 years
articles.title_zh: From Pius XI to Leo XIV: World Mission Day marks 100 years
articles.content_orig:
Pope Pius XI, who served as pope from 1922-1939, created World Mission Sunday in 1926. (CNS/L'Osservatore Romano)
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
For the past 100 years the church has been observing World Mission Day on the second to last Sunday of October. The purpose of the yearly WMD is to help all Catholics (laity, religious, ordained) appreciate the centrality of their mission vocation. Mission is not something the church "does," but rather what the church "is." Vatican II's Ad Gentes says it succinctly: "The pilgrim Church is missionary by her very nature." This message has been stressed annually by all popes, enhancing the WMD event with their messages, inspiration and insights. For WMD 2026, let's take a look at what the last nine popes have said and done to promote the church's missions.
It was this pope who established World Mission Day in 1926, responding to a request from the Society for the Propagation of the Faith. The very first worldwide celebration was held in 1927.  The day is meant to unite Catholics across the globe in responding to their baptismal calling to spread the Gospel and support those communities where the church is young, materially poor, lacking vocations or even persecuted.
In his encyclical Rerum Ecclesiae (1926), which is widely considered the Magna Carta of modern Catholic mission, Pius XI urged bishops worldwide to foster local vocations and promote an Indigenous clergy and religious, rather than relying on foreign missionaries. This task would involve establishing local seminaries and houses of formation, all contributing to planting the church permanently within the local peoples and their cultures. A second encyclical by Pius XI, Rerum Orientalium (1928), focused on promoting missionary activity in the Eastern Catholic Rites.
This papacy occurred during the extremely difficult period of World War II. Probably the most problematic challenge was dealing with Hitler and his persecution of the Jewish people. Untold obstacles had to be addressed as the church sought to remain faithful to her mission. During his papacy Pius XII issued two mission encyclicals: Evangelii Praecones (1951) and Fidei Donum (1957).
Evangelii Praecones ("On Promotion of Catholic Missions") was issued on the 25th anniversary of Pius XI's Rerum Ecclesiae. Despite the interruptions of the Second World War, missionary endeavors achieved a great deal; these are mentioned in the encyclical, especially the growth of Indigenous clergy, religious and bishops. Fidei Donum brought a special emphasis on the church in Africa, especially since many countries there were becoming independent. The goal of mission was slowly but surely being achieved: the establishment firmly and permanently of the local church.
Pope John XXIII (1958-1963)
During his pontificate of less than five years, John XXIII issued eight encyclicals covering topics that included global peace, social justice, human dignity and church unity. He was known as "good Pope John" and is most remembered for convening the Second Vatican Council (1962-1965), which brought significant changes to the church and her mission.
The one specifically missionary encyclical from John XXIII bore the title Princeps Pastorum ("Prince of the Shepherds") (1959). Key emphases of this document centered on the promotion of a native local clergy, the need for self-reliance in local churches, respect for local cultures, and encouragement of laypeople to actively engage in the social mission of the church. Two other documents of John XXIII had deep missionary ramifications: Mater Et Magistra ("Christianity and Social Progress") (1961) spoke of addressing economic imbalances, poverty and the relationship between wealthy and developing nations; Pacem In Terris ("Peace on Earth") (1963) focused on human rights, world peace and international cooperation in the wake of the Cold War and the Cuban missile crisis.
Although Paul VI was not responsible for initiating the Second Vatican Council, he made a remarkable contribution by guiding three sessions and bringing the council to a successful conclusion. Several council documents contributed to a profound renewal of missionary activity, theology and approaches; they are Lumen Gentium , Gaudium Et Spes , Unitatis Redintegratio , Ad Gentes , Apostolicam Actuositatem and Nostra Aetate .
Undoubtedly, the greatest mission contribution of Paul VI was his 1975 apostolic exhortation, Evangelii Nuntiandi ("Evangelization in the Modern World"). This inspiring document renewed the church's missionary focus and cemented the principle that the church exists to evangelize.  The document affirms "evangelizing all people constitutes the essential mission of the Church" and that evangelizing is "the grace and vocation proper to the Church." The document says: "For the Church, evangelizing means bringing the Good News into all strata of humanity."
Paul VI was the first pope to proclaim the World Mission Day Message on radio (Oct. 19, 1963, the Saturday before Mission Sunday). His WMD messages called for unity, peace and the evangelization of the modern world.
Serving only for 33 days, John Paul I was the only pope in modern history who did not issue an annual World Mission Day message. He surprised everyone by choosing two names for his official title; his purpose was to indicate that he intended to continue the renewal fostered by Vatican II that was guided by Popes John XXIII and Paul VI. His affability, humility and contagious joy earned him the popular moniker, "the smiling pope."
Pope John Paul II (1978-2005)
Continuing the use of a double name, this pontiff served for over 26 years, making him the third longest-serving pope in church history. During his pontificate John Paul II issued over two dozen messages for World Mission Day. He consistently emphasized that evangelization is a fundamental duty for all Christians; he urged the faithful to support missionary efforts through a variety of initiatives, including prayer, personal engagement, respect for human dignity and youth involvement. Particularly in the 1990s, his messages spoke of a "new evangelization," designed to reawaken faith and involvement in traditionally Christian areas. His documents included 14 encyclicals, 15 apostolic exhortations, as well as numerous additional writings. His 1990 mission encyclical Redemptoris Missio ("On the Permanent Validity of the Church's Missionary Mandate") presents a comprehensive overview of contemporary evangelization; he starkly proclaims that "Mission is an issue of faith," for without faith no mission is possible!
Pope Benedict XVI (2005-2013)
In modern church history, Benedict is the first pope to resign; he died in 2022. During his pontificate he issued seven World Mission Day messages, striving to show the interconnected themes of Christian charity, Gospel proclamation, global ecclesial communion and involvement of the laity in mission. He did not write an encyclical specifically dedicated to the church's missionary activity. Also, in contrast to his predecessor, Benedict engaged in few international journeys.
Francis is a pope of many firsts, including the first to take the name Francis, first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit pope. He issued 13 annual messages for World Mission Day from 2013-2025, exploring a variety of themes: having a missionary heart, witnessing to mercy, engaging young people, dynamic witnessing, having hearts on fire with feet on the move, being heralds of hope, and living in personal unity with Christ.
Undoubtedly, it was Francis' 2013 apostolic exhortation, Evangelii Gaudium ("The Joy of the Gospel") that marvelously elaborated his profound mission insights. He asserted that "missionary outreach is paradigmatic for all the Church's activity ." He proclaimed: "Throughout the world, let us be 'permanently in a state of mission,' " and that the church must attempt "to put all things in a missionary key." All Christians, he wro

articles.title_orig: Building Bridges between Bangladesh-China through Wikimedia
articles.title_zh: Building Bridges between Bangladesh-China through Wikimedia
articles.content_orig:
How university life in Changsha became an opportunity to bring language, culture, and free knowledge together.
When I moved to Changsha, China to study Electrical Engineering and Automation at Changsha University of Science and Technology (CSUST), I was also thinking of a different kind of infrastructure: the infrastructure of knowledge, language and cultural representation on the internet.
As a polyglot Bengali and Sylheti-speaking student, far away from Bangladesh, the Wikimedia projects were a way to stay connected to my language and be part of a global movement for free knowledge. In 2019, that interest began to take shape beyond individual edits, through in-person gatherings that brought Bangla Wikipedia contributors and Chinese Wikimedians together. In 2020, I was featured by Changsha Evening News for my involvement in promoting cultural exchange between Bangladesh and China as a cultural ambassador .
On 21 February 2019, International Mother Language Day, a Wikimedia gathering took place in front of the Library Complex at CSUST. The event commemorated the martyrs of the Bengali Language Movement and created a space to discuss Wikipedia with two communities in mind: the mainland China Wikipedia community and the Bangla Wikipedia community.
The event is documented on Meta-Wiki , where I was privileged to organise and lead such an initiative. For the first time in its history , the event expanded beyond Bangladesh, demonstrating how the Wikimedia movement can connect language communities across borders . The gathering was also connected to the developing Hunan Wikimedians community, which was created by me in October 2018 .
For me, the significance of the gathering went beyond marking a date on the calendar. International Mother Language Day carries a particular meaning for Bengali speakers: it reminds us that language is bound up with identity, dignity, and the right to be heard. Connecting that history with Wikimedia created an opportunity to talk about how people can preserve and expand their language’s presence in the digital world.
Wikipedia is built through individual contributions, but a contributor community grows when people meet, exchange ideas, and encourage one another to participate.
On 16 December 2019, Bangladesh’s Victory Day, another Bangla Wikipedia gathering took place at CSUST, near the international student dormitory on the Yuntang campus. Bangladeshi students met Chinese Wikimedia contributors to discuss the use of Bangla online, ways to contribute to Wikimedia projects, and opportunities for cultural exchange.
I documented the gathering in a report for Prothom Alo . It was the second such gathering organised by me at the university in 2019, following the February event.
The December meeting even more highlighted the importance of local context in Wikimedia outreach. However, in practice, Participation was difficult because Wikipedia was blocked in mainland China at the time. In the meantime, I could manage the Global IP block exemptions to ensure that I can continue my contributions smoothly across all Wikimedia projects. When talking about these realities with people from different language communities, the conversation about contribution brought the conversation back down to the ground in the realities people actually faced.
It was about more than editing an encyclopedia. It was also about helping people learn about each other’s histories and cultures. On Bangladesh’s Victory Day, the participants welcomed each other and talked about Bangladesh’s Liberation War and how cultural exchange can continue.
Thinking back on my experience at CSUST I realised that, contributing to Wikimedia can be more than just writing or editing articles. It can also mean helping people find a project, creating opportunities for contributors to connect, documenting community activities, and building bridges between language communities.
Although these activities were insufficient in terms of size , they were set in a meaningful context: a university in China where students from different countries lived and studied together. That environment facilitated a combination between the local experience and the global movement.
Since then my work with Bangla Wikimedia projects and work supporting Sylheti language representation has continued to deepen my interest in linguistic diversity. At its heart, the question remains the same: how can communities make their knowledge, histories and languages more visible and accessible to the online world?
From that time, I also began translating and reshaping Wikipedia articles into news reports aimed at a broader audience beyond Wikipedia. These reports were started to be published in various Bangladeshi newspapers, including Prothom Alo , Jugantor , The Financial Express , and others . In 2021, I was awarded the BCYSA Outstanding Journalist Award for my work that showed a dedicated effort to document communities, preserve cultural knowledge, and translate information across languages.
My experience in Changsha showed me that this work needs both digital inputs and human connections. An edit might add a fact to an article, a gathering can introduce someone to the community that keeps knowledge growing.
My role as the Campus Director for the Hult Prize at Changsha University of Science and Technology was a constant combination of multilingual communication, education, and community building within the Wikimedia movement and in global academic settings. In June 2022, I was officially appointed as a 2022 Alumni Liaison (校友联络员) for the International College of Changsha University of Science and Technology, and ended up with my Changsha chapter.
One simple lesson from my experience for Wikimedia contributors working in smaller and under-represented language communities: start with the people around you . A university campus, a cultural event, or a conversation between speakers of different languages can be an entry point to free knowledge. The first step might be a small get-together, but the relationships formed can endure long after the event has ended.
In order for this article to reach as many people as possible we would like your help. Can you translate this article to get the message out?

articles.title_orig: Japan to launch world-first mission to collect samples from Martian moon
articles.title_zh: Japan to launch world-first mission to collect samples from Martian moon
articles.content_orig:
Japanese space agency leading five-year mission to Phobos, one of ‘most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system’
Japan is to launch a spacecraft on the world’s first mission to bring back samples from Phobos, one of the two small, potato-shaped moons orbiting Mars.
Scientists hope the mission, which is expected to take five years, will provide clues to how Phobos and its smaller sibling Deimos formed, and hopefully even shed light on the origins of life in the solar system.
The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa) is aiming to launch the spacecraft on Tuesday on a new Japanese mainstay H3 rocket.
Yasuhiro Kawakatsu, project manager for the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission, said samples from Phobos would provide useful data for scientists to consider using a Martian moon as a base for a future manned mission to the planet. The US, China and others are hoping to send astronauts to Mars .
“Despite their potential importance, Martian moons have never been fully investigated,” Kawakatsu said. “They are known as the most important unclimbed mountains in the solar system.”
Japan is leading an international mission, which includes equipment and communications support from Nasa and other national space agencies.
Since the 1960s, dozens of missions have been sent to Mars, but its moons largely remain a mystery. Multiple Russian attempts to land on Phobos, including one launched in 2011, have failed.
Phobos and Deimos take their names from the Greek mythological personifications of fear and terror, sons of the war god Ares, whose Roman counterpart is Mars.
A key question is how they formed and what they are made of. Some scientists think the two irregular crater-pocked bodies could be remnants of debris formed after a large celestial object crashed into Mars. Others say the moons could be asteroids that have come from elsewhere.
Jaxa officials think samples from Phobos will provide answers. “We can almost certainly come to a conclusion by analysing soil samples,” said Kiyoshi Kuramoto, principal investigator on the mission.
Scientists chose to collect samples from Phobos mainly because the moon is closer to Mars than Deimos, and therefore may have more information about the planet. Material from Mars is expected to make up about 0.1% of the material collected from Phobos, Jaxa officials say.
Phobos is about 27km (17 miles) in diameter at its widest point, and orbits Mars at a distance of about 6,000km (3,700 miles) three times a day.
Samples from Phobos could also shed light on the origin of Deimos as the two moons were believed to have similar roots, Kuramoto said. The mission includes plans to fly by Deimos and collect observations.
It will be a long journey to reach the red planet, which is 55m km away from Earth at its closest point. The actual flight distance would be 500-600m km, Kawakatsu said.
After launching on the H3 rocket, the spacecraft will arrive at the Mars region in around August 2027. It will then fly near and around Phobos for three years to collect data and samples from the moon, before returning home in 2031.
MMX is made up of three modules, for propulsion, exploration and return. Only the third module will return home with the samples.
The spacecraft will carry 13 instruments, including a rover jointly developed by France and Germany that will land on the moon, as well as a Nasa sampling device and instrument to measure gamma rays, and the European Space Agency’s deep space communication device. A Japanese radiation monitor will collect data that can help a future manned Mars exploration.
The French-German rover Idefix is due to on Phobos first. During a 100-day mission in around 2029, it will explore the surface to help the subsequent Japanese soil-sampling. The spacecraft will choose a relatively smooth and level site for its landing based on topographical data provided by the rover.
Once the MMX mission lands, Jaxa scientists aim to collect at least 10g (0.35oz) of soil from the moon from two sampling attempts using US and Japanese methods.
Nasa’s sampling device uses pressurised gas to lift surface dust into a container, and Jaxa’s coring method will collect samples from a depth of about 2cm. In the first attempt, the MMX will collect surface and underground samples using both devices, and take additional underground samples in the second landing.
Scientists say collecting samples from multiple locations increases the chances of obtaining any potential traces of past microbial life from Mars .
Landing on the pockmarked moon, which has just one two-thousandths of Earth’s gravity, is a challenge. To minimise bouncing at touchdown, the MMX’s exploration module is equipped with four-legged landing gear with shock absorption features.
The rover has wheels that can get traction in low gravity, right itself if it tips over, and move “at a snail’s pace”, according to Jaxa.
The samples will be stored in a heat-protected capsule designed to survive reentry into Earth’s atmosphere. The module is expected to land in Australia before being sent back to Japan.

Read all of our coverage of Maine's 2026 election or stay up to date with the latest developments through the Maine Political Report in your inbox or text messages from politics editor Kirby Wilson.
Having voted since 1968, I find my election cynicism at a demoralizing level this year.
It’s hard to point to one thing that has hardened my cynicism, but the obscene concentration of wealth tops my list.
Our version of capitalism has given Elon Musk personal wealth greater than the GDP of 174 nations, while 86 million live in poverty or near poverty. There are many ultra-wealthy not far behind him and, with the carte blanche of Citizens United, that wealth has exponentially increased influence. We are now in a “post-government” world, where wealthy oligarchs make the decisions regardless of electoral outcomes. Who do they answer to?
We witnessed an example of “post-government” recently when President Trump had the AI billionaires to the White House to discuss AI regulation. The solution? No regulation. Let the geniuses regulate themselves. The most threatening technology since the atom bomb. But trust them.

articles.title_orig: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at Canadian military base
articles.title_zh: Major fire breaks out in Alberta after deadly incident at Canadian military base
articles.content_orig:
Canada’s defense minister says that people have been killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, while reports said that large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals
EDMONTON, Alberta -- Canada’s defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, while reports said that large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals.
Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.
It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km (120 miles) northwest, told Canada’s national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became “completely overwhelmed” by the number of people needing care.
“This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton,” Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.”
The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.
Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as “very, very active and delicate.” He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.
Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.
By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.
“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as “significant and tragic” and said it was affecting many military personnel.
CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.
Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.
“Pray for Wainwright, everyone,” Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.
The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada . Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

articles.title_orig: French police arrest 855 people in Paris as protests, violence erupt across country
articles.title_zh: French police arrest 855 people in Paris as protests, violence erupt across country
articles.content_orig:
France's interior minister said on Sunday more than 1,800 people were arrested during and after protests on Saturday and in a separate statement, french police said they had detained a record 855 people in Paris alone over violence, amid nationwide demonstrations.
Cars were set on fire and shops were looted in Paris on Saturday as police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse violent protesters who joined protests against rising living costs and in support of high school students' grievances .
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's said in a post on Sunday that "1,800 people have been arrested and now investigations are under way to identify the perpetrators of these acts so they can be brought to justice."
Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the "yellow vest" movement , which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Demonstrators expressed widespread frustration and anger at the government as gasoline, energy and food prices have spiked in recent months.
Police fired tear gas and water cannons to push back people wearing hoods and masks and throwing fireworks, paving stones and other objects at officers in the Place de la République, northeast of the Paris city center.
Associated Press reporters saw thick black smoke rising from cars, bicycles and other vehicles, and trash bins on fire. A kiosk was also burning, while several shops have been looted. Several people have been injured in the clashes.
Alexandre Bompard, the head of a french retail group said on Sunday that around 1,500 ships and retailers were damaged in the protests over the weekend, with many of them looted, causing "several hundreds of millions of euros" in damage
Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.
Meanwhile, the majority of peaceful protesters joined a march that moved toward northwestern Paris. The crowd chanted France's national anthem and waved flags, and some people played trumpets and violins.
In Lyon, France's third-largest city, where about 20,000 protesters joined the march, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In the southwestern city of Limoges, the region's top official said masked protesters broke into and set fire to a town hall building, causing the spire to collapse in flames. "A wild horde" had "deliberately" set fire to the 143-year-old building, whose roof largely collapsed during Saturday's protests, Maurice Barate, prefect for the Haute-Vienne department, told TV news channel LCI.
In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall.
"This is unacceptable," Marseille Mayor Benoît Payan told BFM TV, describing the damage in City Hall as "limited."
Nuñez's office also reported violence by masked groups in Rennes, Toulouse, Montpellier and Grenoble, among other cities.
Sonia Mabrouk, 40, said she came from a suburb west of Paris with her daughter, a high school student, to protest "everything that's going wrong," particularly the neglect of public services. Mabrouk, who took part in the yellow vest protests, criticized "policies that favor the rich and always hit the poorest people in their wallets."
Many protesters could be seen wearing the fluorescent yellow vests that became a symbol of the 2018 rallies. "There's a general sense of frustration and anger," Mabrouk said, as she marched alongside peaceful demonstrators of all ages.
Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them.
The CGT, one of France's major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for "higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people's needs."
It said that over 500,000 protesters joined the rallies Saturday.
In recent weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country's presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon , who backed the high school students' movement, also took part in the Paris protest Saturday.
Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand.

articles.title_orig: US ambassador urges Israel to prosecute attackers of American journalist
articles.title_zh: US ambassador urges Israel to prosecute attackers of American journalist
articles.content_orig:
United States Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has demanded Israel prosecute and jail those responsible for the attack on American journalist Heidi Levine in the occupied West Bank, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington wants Israel to do more to deter settler attacks.
“Attacking a female photographer is a despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards,” Huckabee wrote on X on Saturday.
“Those who attacked unarmed reporter should spend YRS in prison,” he added. “We have called for a full investigation, arrest, and prosecution to the fullest extent of the law to whoever participated in this.”
Rubio said on Saturday that the US State Department had inquired about the attack on Levine and that he expected to hear back from the US embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday.
“We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing,” he told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff.”
⁠Rubio’s comments to reporters came after the widespread dissemination of video showing settlers attacking Levine, a photojournalist with The Washington Post.
Rubio said the administration of US President Donald Trump would communicate its expectations to the Israelis “to prevent that from happening in the future”.
“We don’t need that right now; Israel doesn’t need that right now,” he added.
Levine was covering Palestinians’ annual olive harvest on Friday in the occupied West Bank when Israeli settlers brutally attacked her and several Palestinians.
Israeli settlers stormed the area, beat her and stole her passport, telephone, wallet and equipment, according to witnesses.
The perpetrators, armed with bottles and slingshots, “were kicking me for like 10 minutes, and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag”, Levine said.
Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera that Levine “was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground.”
Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah.
The American photojournalist underwent surgery on her finger, which was nearly detached from her hand, and was left with a broken rib and multiple broken vertebrae, as well as lacerations, her daughter told The Associated Press news agency.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who wants to shore up his pro-settlement right-wing base ahead of closely fought October 27 elections, claimed on Friday that Palestinians or “far-left” activists may have been responsible for the attack on Levine and other Palestinians.
Meanwhile, Ambassador Huckabee, a staunch ally of Israel who has sharply criticised Israeli settler attacks against Americans, did not identify the culprits as settlers after Netanyahu tried to sow doubt as to their identity.
The Trump-appointed ambassador met Palestinian-Americans in the occupied West Bank town of Turmus Aya in September to hear locals’ testimony about their experiences with pogroms. In August, Huckabee called a days-long Israeli settler siege an “act of terror”.
The State Department criticised Friday’s attack using a cautious tone on Levine’s beating, stating condemnation of “criminal violence by any party”.
Israeli settlers have been involved in at least 170 pogroms against Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli group that monitors illegal Israeli settlements.

articles.title_orig: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,200 arrested
articles.title_zh: France protests: Violent clashes, looting and buildings ablaze as over 1,200 arrested
articles.content_orig:
Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against hardship in schools and the cost of living.
At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence" alongside an estimated 550,000 taking to the streets.
In Paris, there were significant clashes into the evening with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon on crowds.
Buildings were set alight in the capital and other areas, including in Limoges where a large fire in the town hall caused the roof to partly collapse.
Looting broke out in several cities, with widespread vandalism targeting city halls and businesses also reported.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said 150 police officers were injured in the unrest.
In the French capital, the main march appeared to be largely peaceful during the afternoon. A group of young people told the BBC that they were "pacifists" who were "just trying to make things change, but nothing is moving".
However, as the day wore on some groups lit fires in the street and torched vehicles, including in iconic locations in the city centre like the Place de la République.
Shops were ransacked, at least one restaurant was gutted by fire, and the BBC saw fighting breaking out among some of the groups.
Riot police were seen charging at one crowd in central Paris and hitting several people with batons.
In Lyon, Mayor Grégory Doucet said the burning of the city's tourist office was "a tragedy", telling BFMTV "it breaks our hearts because it's a very iconic, well-known historic building".
Local police said "hostile individuals" prevented firefighters from safely tackling the blaze.
Fire crews also battled the fire at Limoges town hall, which the local prefecture said caused part of the building to collapse.
A young man "had his hand blown off" by a small explosive in Saint-Étienne, the south-eastern city's Mayor Régis Juanico said on social media, adding: "Such a tragedy should never have happened."
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested in recent weeks over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées - secondary schools attended by 15- to 18-year-olds.
Their numbers have been bolstered by trade union members and other protest groups.
These groups include the so-called gilets jaunes (or "yellow vest") movement, which demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for more than a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
France's interior ministry said Saturday's protests involved "targeted acts of violence" from "hooded individuals" in places, including parts of the capital and also Marseille, Rennes, Toulouse and Angers.
Damage to buildings was reported across France, including in Grenoble, Avignon, Pau, Montpellier and Valence.
Clothes and food shops were raided in Paris, while an Apple store in Lille was broken into and emptied.
Footage authenticated by BBC Verify showed a tourist train in Grenoble being driven by masked men along a narrow street in the city centre towards at least three riot police officers.
While France is no stranger to outbreaks of protest and disorder, this round comes as the country heads into a period of deep political uncertainty.
French President Emmanuel Macron will leave office next year and polls suggest April's presidential election could come down to a fight between the leader of the National Rally, Marine Le Pen, and Jean-Luc Mélenchon of the hard-left La France Insoumise party.
The latter took part in demonstrations in France and later accused police officers of "unleashing" on protesters, while condemning looting and arson.
Lecornu said his comments were "dangerous and cynical".
He earlier said police had faced "violence of extreme intensity" and some groups were using the protests as a "warm-up" for the presidential elections, adding: "No-one will impose their political agenda through violence."
Le Pen said "legitimate demands" voiced by protesters had been "held hostage by the far left", accusing Mélenchon of fuelling the violence.
Macron said: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."
The government has made apparent attempts at concessions, with Education Minister Édouard Geffray promising 3,000 extra supply teachers during a television interview on 8 October.
However, the protests have continued and intensified.

articles.title_orig: Zacharia posts altered photos of Trump’s Oval Office desk
articles.title_zh: Zacharia posts altered photos of Trump’s Oval Office desk
articles.content_orig:
Settling in for a seven-hour flight across the continent this week, President Donald Trump offered little indication there was anything wrong.
His new press secretary’s rocky 14-minute debut at the White House podium was being met with decidedly negative reviews . An hour later, she’d offered a perplexing response when asked where she’d passed the bar exam. His own advisers had watched it all with a degree of horror.
Trump, however, told Katie Zacharia on the flight to Alaska that she performed well, a source familiar with the conversation told CNN. It was her first time on Air Force One.
Three days and an onslaught of scrutiny later, Zacharia was dismissed from her post, summarily ending the shortest stint as White House press secretary in anyone’s memory. Plans to move east from California with her family were put on hold. It was all, multiple Trump advisers said, a real flop.
“I said, ‘Is this for you, Katie?’” Trump said Friday, after he’d fired her. “Because honestly, you don’t need this.”
The entire episode underscored the uneasy atmosphere that has pervaded Trump’s inner circle less than three weeks before the midterm elections. Zacharia’s sudden hiring and equally swift firing were a product of Trump’s impulse to hire a loyal television defender he’d grown somewhat enamored with from afar, without much thought to the other requirements of the job.
In a statement for this story, White House Communications Director Steven Cheung said: “All of this breathless speculation is just that— speculation. And it’s fiction that’s not even creative. The fact is that Katie took on a very important job, and she will continue to support the President as she transitions to a new role. She is an amazing teammate and tremendous talent.”
CNN has reached out to Zacharia for comment. In a post on X , she said it “was an honor” to work for Trump.
I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to,” she wrote.
Some Trump advisers watched her brief tenure unfold with a measure of chagrin, wondering how one of the government’s most visible and sought-after jobs could have gone to someone with so little experience or confidence in performing it.
“What the f**k is happening over there?” one Trump adviser asked incredulously after watching the newly installed Zacharia conduct her first, widely panned press briefing.
The new press secretary, multiple advisers said, appeared woefully underprepared — and lacked basic skills to do the job.
“Did anyone vet her?” one asked.
The short answer, it turned out, was no, according to multiple White House officials and advisers.
Instead, her selection came amid a burst of frustration on the part of the president that a month ahead of the midterms, there were few voices defending him amid unrelenting coverage of Republicans’ dwindling midterm prospects.
Until that point, the president had shown no real urgency in filling the role Karoline Leavitt vacated at the end of the summer. Advisers and allies had floated names, none of which seemed to seriously pique Trump’s interest. White House officials had become resigned to the possibility there would be no press secretary before the midterms.
But the intensifying political problems for Republicans — and the blame Trump was catching for the party’s woes — appeared to kickstart his search. After struggling for weeks to land a new press secretary, Trump suddenly became fixated on filling the role, complaining to advisers he had no one pushing his message, multiple sources familiar with the matter said.
Into that anger emerged a benevolent voice: Zacharia, cable news regular, passionate defender, sometimes labeled an attorney on TV. What about Katie? Trump asked advisers, including chief of staff Susie Wiles, a source familiar with the matter said. The president also sought Leavitt’s counsel.
Only a week earlier, Zacharia was not being considered for the role. Throughout the search to replace Leavitt, the White House struggled with higher-profile names, several of whom had previously criticized Trump. On multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list, only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position, according a White House official.
Zacharia’s record was “unblemished,” Trump would later say. Among her boosters in the West Wing was Natalie Harp , the loyal Trump aide who travels with him everywhere, a source familiar with the matter said.
On Wednesday last week, officials arranged a phone call between Zacharia and the president. Zacharia flew to Washington a day later. By Friday, she was in the Oval Office.
During their conversation, which Wiles was not present for, Trump spontaneously offered Zacharia the job, a source familiar with the matter said. Aides rushed to inform Wiles of the decision.
“I got a wonderful phone call from the chief talent recruiter, the president himself, and it turns out that being a huge supporter of all of his policies actually works,” Zacharia said during a Fox News interview last Friday evening.
That interview aired at the same time Trump was speaking at a rally in Syracuse, New York. For some longtime Trump advisers, it was the first sign of trouble. Counter-programming the president’s events with a TV hit has long been seen as a faux pas for underlings — including for Cabinet officials and top administration officials.
If Trump noticed, however, he didn’t let on. By Sunday evening, he announced Zacharia would convene her first “introductory” briefing bright and early Tuesday morning.
After another round-trip flight between Washington and California, Zacharia was up at 3 a.m. Tuesday to prepare. Her materials weren’t finalized until 90 minutes before she walked into the briefing room.
The lack of preparation showed. Her delivery during the opening was halting, even though she was reading from a laudatory boilerplate script about Trump’s record.
“Some people have it and some people do not,” one senior administration official said. “She does not. She couldn’t command the room.”
When the time came for questions, she didn’t know whether the US had cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine — an inquiry that could have easily been anticipated.
She did announce that Kimberly Guilfoyle had been asked to resign from her post as ambassador to Greece, which Zacharia later used as an example of how successful the outing had been.
“I think I’m one of the first press secretaries to deliver staff changes for the administration,” she said later in the week, as her future was becoming increasingly bleak. “And I was honored that President Trump trusted me delivering that information.”
That would end up being the only real information she delivered in the job.
Though Trump did not initially think her performance at her first press briefing was particularly bad, he later became embarrassed by the coverage.
Other signs also emerged of Zacharia’s inexperience. During Trump’s visit to Alaska following her maligned briefing, a source familiar with the matter said, Zacharia told White House officials she planned an interview for the president with a Fox News reporter following the rally. But she was quickly warned the president didn’t like to do anything after his events, having just performed for two hours. The preference was well known among Trump’s team.
Zacharia insisted it would be wise, and that the reporter was a friend, the source said. After Trump got off the stage and was ready to depart, Zacharia told him of the plan. Trump grew visibly irritated and said he wasn’t going to do it, the source said. Ultimately, he relented, but the episode was indicative to those around him that Zacharia did not yet understand the man she now worked for.
